title: The Reading
subtitle: Sunday 15 to Tuesday 17 October 1893: A Will by Gaslight, a Lamp in the Closed Wing, a Door That Tries Itself

setting.name: Greywick House and Haverkill station, the first two nights
setting.description: The party arrives on the 4:12 from New York on Sunday afternoon, is driven up the hill to Greywick House, and at eight o'clock hears Jasper Greywick's will read by gaslight in the library: seven nights under this roof or forfeit, a sealed codicil for the eighth morning, and bequests that make no sense to anyone. Then Mrs. Quell collects every bedroom key. The first night is quiet and wrong. On Monday the house shows its people: a widow who is kindness itself, a son who wants to break the will, a lawyer who will not open his box, a housekeeper who lights a lamp in a window nobody uses; and a parlourmaid finds a wet umbrella and a valise in the hall closet that belong to the heir who never came. On Monday night Conrad Greywick locks his door. Everything the players need to know about Rule 1, and the first thread toward Linus, is in these two nights, for anyone who asks why the keys were taken.
setting.atmosphere: Mourning and money. Black crape on the hall mirror and the knocker; the gasoliers hissing; a fire in every grate and still a cold that comes up from the floors. The library smells of leather, coal smoke and the lilies left over from the funeral. The household speaks in lowered voices and watches each other do sums. Outside it is clear and very cold, with a half moon on the river and the Catskills black against the stars; the night boat to Albany goes by at ten with its lights blazing and its paddles thrashing, and the river line freight rumbles along the water at midnight. At three the hall clock strikes and every sleeper in the house wakes and listens. In the north wing, through a gap in the curtains, the lamp in the river window burns all night.

keyLocations.name: The Library
keyLocations.description: Two storeys of books with an iron gallery and a spiral stair, three tall Gothic windows over the terrace and the river, a long table where the will is read, leather chairs, a marble fireplace with Abram Greywick's portrait above it, and two brass gasoliers. In the panelled east wall is the steel door of the strongroom, where the family papers, the plate and the deed boxes are kept; Mr. Strick has the strongroom key for the week, and the black japanned dispatch box with the will and the sealed codicil goes everywhere with him.
features: Abram Greywick's portrait: a heavy, clever man of fifty with river-grey eyes, one hand on a rolled plan of a railroad and the other on an iron key lying on the table beside him

The strongroom: a steel door, shelves of deed boxes, the Greywick plate, and on a hook by the door a board of house keys with every hook labelled, one of them empty and marked 'North Wing, River Room'

Mr. Strick's dispatch box: black japanned tin, brass corners, a lock whose key hangs on the lawyer's watch chain, and a red wax seal visible through the open lid on a long envelope marked 'CODICIL. Not to be opened before 9 o'clock a.m., 22nd October 1893'
The register: a ledger on a stand in the hall outside, ruled in Cyprian Tunstall's neat hand, with a column for each named person and each night, to be signed at sunset and sunrise
encounters: The reading at eight: Leonora, Conrad, Honora (if not a player), Ellis Callender, Dr. Wyle, Mrs. Tierney, Miss Oudekerk, Mr. Strick, Cyprian Tunstall, and, standing at the back, Mrs. Quell and Gerrit Brouwer
Conrad Greywick after the reading, demanding Strick tell him what is in the codicil
secrets: CLUE E (partial): the will leaves 'my gold watch and chain, with what hangs upon it, to my son Linus'. Strick lists the effects afterwards: a gold hunter watch, a chain, a seal, and 'a small old iron key of no value'. Leonora says gently that she has the watch in her keeping for Linus. She has the watch; the key is in her workbasket.

CLUE A2 (core): every invitation carried a postscript in Jasper's own shaking hand: 'Do not lock your door.' Strick says Jasper insisted on writing it himself on each letter in the last week of his life, 'a fancy of his illness'. Strick does not believe in ghosts. He also does not lock his door.

Strick will not open the codicil before the hour on any account. Insight DC 13: he knows what is in it, and it frightens him. Persuasion DC 18 (advantage for Cyprian, his own clerk): he says only that 'Mr. Greywick wished to make a restitution, and to make it in a manner I advised against.'

Insight DC 14 during the reading: when Strick reads the Fourth article ('I ask it as it was once asked of another'), Mrs. Quell, at the back, shuts her eyes; Leonora does not look up from her gloves; and the gas in both gasoliers sinks and blue-flickers for the length of a breath and rises again. Nobody touched the taps.

keyLocations.name: The Great Hall, the Hall Closet and the Blue Room
keyLocations.description: The great hall rises the full height of the house to a timbered roof, with a staircase climbing round three sides to the first-floor gallery, a stone fireplace, the long-case clock, a hall stand of antlers and umbrellas, and the register on its stand. The south corridor runs off the gallery to the guest rooms; the Blue Room is the first door, looking out over the drive. It is made up, aired, and, Leonora says, kept for Linus.
features: The hall closet under the stairs: coats, galoshes, a croquet set, and, behind the coats, a pigskin valise with the initials L.J.G. and a Chicago hotel label, and a man's black umbrella still damp at the ferrule
The hall clock: it strikes three at three, and everyone awake in the house hears it

The Blue Room: blue toile, a brass bed whose sheets have been changed (by Leonora herself, Fanny says, which no lady does), a washstand, a wardrobe, a keyhole with no key, and a faint smell of wet wool
Mrs. Quell's key board in the servants' hall: a hook for every bedroom, every key hung on the first night; the hook for the Blue Room was empty before the guests came
encounters: Fanny Ruddock, the parlourmaid, on Monday morning, holding a damp umbrella and wondering whether to say anything
Leonora Greywick, arranging flowers in the hall, who sees everything that happens there
secrets: CLUE C1 (core, Monday morning, for anyone Fanny tells or who looks in the closet): the valise and umbrella. The valise is locked (Mechanics DC 12 or a pocket knife and no scruples). Inside: a man's clothes for a week, a Chicago newspaper of 12 October, a draughtsman's case, and a letter.

CLUE A4, E5 and C (core, in the valise): Jasper's letter to Linus of 20 September: 'My dear boy. Come up the day before the reading if you can; there are things I must say and cannot write. Never lock a door in this house at night, whatever anyone tells you, and if anything happens to me before you come, the key is on my chain; you will know what it is for when Gerrit tells you. I have told Leonora what I mean to do. She took it badly, and I do not blame her. You will hate me a little when you hear it. Her name was ... no. I will say it to your face. Your father, J.' Leonora will say, if shown it, that Jasper was very ill in his last weeks and frightened of everything.

CLUE C6 (core for anyone who looks at the Blue Room's bed or asks Fanny): the bed was slept in on Saturday night, and Mrs. Greywick changed the sheets herself on Sunday before the guests came. The Blue Room's key is not on Mrs. Quell's board and was not there on Saturday afternoon either; Mrs. Quell assumed Mrs. Greywick had it. Leonora says Linus has not come, and the room was aired for him.

Leonora will explain the valise smoothly if challenged: Linus sent his luggage ahead by express and will follow. Insight DC 15 sees that this is the first lie she has had to make up on the spot. There is no express receipt.

keyLocations.name: The North Wing Door and the River Lamp
keyLocations.description: At the north end of the first-floor gallery a short passage ends at a low oak door, much older than the house round it, set into a wall of rough stone. It is locked by day, with nobody behind it. Beyond it a steep enclosed stair climbs to the river room. The ground-floor door to the cellar kitchen is at the end of the service passage behind the dining room, also locked. At dusk every day Mrs. Quell unlocks the gallery door, carries a lit kerosene lamp up the stair, sets it in the river window, comes down, and locks the door again.
features: The gallery door: oak, iron-strapped, a modern lock fitted in 1858, cold to the touch even in daylight
The lamp: a brass kerosene lamp with a glass chimney, filled each evening from a can in the scullery; from the terrace and the drive the window shows a steady yellow light all night
The iron wedges: on the threshold of every bedroom in the house, a black iron door wedge, heavier than a wedge needs to be
encounters: Mrs. Quell with the lamp at dusk on Sunday and Monday, who will not be hurried and will not answer questions on the stair

Night 1, about three: whoever is awake and near the gallery hears, from beyond the north wing door, a man's voice, hoarse and far away, calling 'Honora? Honora, is that you?' (fear check DC 10; Honora, if played, DC 15)
secrets: CLUE B1 (core, automatic for anyone who watches at dusk): the lamp. Mrs. Quell says only that 'Mr. Jasper wished a lamp kept there, and Mr. Abram before him. It is for the river.' Persuasion DC 15: 'Mr. Jasper's orders. I have lit it every night for twenty-seven years. As long as it burns, the house is quiet.' She will say no more on Sunday or Monday.

CLUE B2 (core): the iron wedges. Mrs. Quell says they are for the draughts. Gerrit Brouwer, asked, says 'Ask Mrs. Quell' and goes red. Occult DC 12 (Cyprian has advantage): iron across a threshold is old folk practice against things that come through doors; in Dutch river lore, against things that shut them.

CLUE C4 (Night 1): the voice is Linus Greywick's, from the river room as it was in 1852. Honora knows her brother's voice. If anyone calls back, the voice stops, and after a long time says, 'Is it night? She says it is still night.' Then nothing. By day the door is just a locked door and the stair beyond it is empty, and Mrs. Quell has the key.

If anyone gets through the gallery door at night (Mrs. Quell's key, or Mechanics DC 15), the stair is very cold and the river room's oak door at the top is locked and will not open for anything; its keyhole is furred with frost. Fear check DC 10. This is Rule 3 in plain sight, and the players will not yet know it.

keyLocations.name: The Servants' Hall
keyLocations.description: A long, warm, stone-floored room below stairs with a deal table, a range, the bell board, Mrs. Quell's key board and her sitting room off it. The household eats here at noon: Mrs. Quell at the head, Mrs. Jansen the cook, Jem Kittering the footman, the coachman, two housemaids, Fanny Ruddock the parlourmaid, and Gerrit Brouwer when he comes in from the grounds. They have all been told the same thing: no locked doors, and nobody goes in the north wing.
features: Mrs. Quell's key board, every hook labelled, every bedroom key hung on Sunday night
The bell board, whose bell for the north wing's river room was disconnected years ago and still rings, very faintly, some nights
Mrs. Jansen's kitchen, where coffee is always on and gossip is free to anyone who dries a plate
encounters: The servants at their noon dinner, polite to the family, open to anyone who sits down with them
Fanny Ruddock, who has a secret of her own and wants to know which of the guests she can trust
secrets: CLUE A1 (core): asked about the keys, any servant says the same thing: Mr. Jasper never allowed a locked door after dark, not in forty years, and Mrs. Quell takes the keys of anyone new. Jem the footman adds that Mr. Abram died in '73 because he bolted himself in his study; 'everybody in Haverkill knows that, sir, only they say apoplexy.'

The north wing bell rang on the night of Saturday 14 October, at about three, Mrs. Jansen says; it has rung every night since, faintly. It also rang every night from 24 September to 30 September, she says, and then stopped. She has told nobody because nobody asked.

Fanny will tell the party about the umbrella (CLUE C1) if they are kind to her; she will not yet tell them what she saw on 24 September (CLUE G4, gw-scenario-002): Insight DC 14 sees there is something more, and that she is afraid of Mrs. Greywick.

Gerrit Brouwer knows the most and says the least. Insight DC 13: he flinches whenever anyone mentions locking a door. His story waits for gw-scenario-002, or for a party that asks him straight out, by daylight, away from the house.

keyLocations.name: Haverkill Station and the Telegraph Office
keyLocations.description: A board-and-batten station on the river flats at the foot of the hill, beside the freight yards of the Haverkill & Berkshire, with a waiting room, a ticket window, a stove, the station agent's office and the Western Union instrument. Mr. Amzi Peake, the agent, has been here twenty years and sees every passenger.
features: The telegraph book, in which every message in and out is copied
The ticket stubs from Saturday's trains, spiked on a nail in the agent's office
The view up the hill to the house, and the lamp in the north window, which the agent has seen every night for twenty years
encounters: Mr. Peake, slow, kindly and proud of his memory
secrets: CLUE C3 (core for anyone who asks): no telegram from Linus Greywick, or from anyone in Chicago, has come to Haverkill since 1 October. The only telegrams to the house were condolences and Mr. Strick's.

CLUE C2 (core for anyone who asks about Saturday's trains): Mr. Peake took a Chicago through-ticket from a young gentleman off the last up train, 10:38 on Saturday night, in the rain, and told him the way up the hill since there was no carriage. 'Said his name was Greywick. Looked like the old man, round the eyes.' The stub is on the nail.

Peake also remembers, without being asked, that the lamp in the north window went out once, in October 1873, for a week, 'the week old Mr. Abram died', and that the river men have always said that a lit window up there means 'the captain's home'. He does not know which captain.

synopsis: The party arrives at Haverkill on Sunday afternoon and hears Jasper Greywick's will read by gaslight: seven nights under Greywick's roof or forfeit, a sealed codicil for the morning of 22 October, an iron key 'of no value' on the watch chain left to an absent son, and odd bequests to a doctor, a medium, a lawyer's clerk and a farm woman nobody knows. Mrs. Quell takes every bedroom key, carries a lamp up into the closed north wing, and will not say why. On the first night a man's voice calls through the north wing door. On Monday the household shows itself, and Fanny Ruddock finds Linus Greywick's umbrella and valise in the hall closet, with his father's letter: never lock a door at night; the key is on my chain; I have told Leonora what I mean to do. Linus, Leonora says, has not come. On Monday night Conrad Greywick, drunk, furious and sure someone means to rob him, locks his door, and at three the handle tries itself, the keyhole frosts over and something begins to scratch at the bottom of the door. If the party gets him out before the clock finishes striking, he lives, and will not say what he saw. By Tuesday morning the party should know that a locked door calls something in this house, that the lamp and the iron matter, and that Linus Greywick came up the hill on Saturday night and is still somewhere in the house.
hook: Eight o'clock, the library, gaslight. Mr. Lemuel Strick unlocks his black box, unfolds the will, settles his spectacles, and looks round the long table at the people the dead man has gathered: the widow in black silk, a red-faced son, a daughter in grey, a broad young man in a fireman's coat, a country doctor, a woman in a theatrical hat, a farm woman with her hands in her lap, his own clerk, and the servants standing at the back. One chair is empty. 'Mr. Linus Greywick,' says Strick, 'has telegraphed that he is delayed. Mrs. Greywick tells me so.' He clears his throat. 'Very well. I, Jasper Abram Greywick, of Greywick House in the Town of Haverkill...'

conclusions.conclusion: A. A locked door at night calls something in this house (Rule 1)
clues: A1: Mrs. Quell takes the keys; the servants say Mr. Jasper never allowed a locked door after dark (the servants' hall)
A2: 'Do not lock your door' in Jasper's hand on every invitation (the library, Strick)
A3: Conrad's locked door on Monday night (the south corridor)
A4: Jasper's letter to Linus (the hall closet)

conclusions.conclusion: C. Linus Greywick came on Saturday night and is in the house
clues: C1: his valise and wet umbrella in the hall closet (Fanny, the hall)
C2: the station agent took his ticket off the 10:38 on Saturday (the station)
C3: there was no telegram (the telegraph book)
C4: his voice behind the north wing door at three (the gallery)
C6: the Blue Room slept in and its sheets changed by Leonora; its key missing (the Blue Room, Fanny, Mrs. Quell)

conclusions.conclusion: B. The lamp and the iron matter (Rule 2, first half)
clues: B1: Mrs. Quell's lamp in the river window, every dusk (the north wing door)
B2: the iron wedges on every threshold (every bedroom)
Peake: 'a lit window up there means the captain's home' (the station)
Mrs. Quell, pressed: 'As long as it burns, the house is quiet' (the stair)

acts.title: Sunday: The Will by Gaslight
acts.description: Arrival, the reading and the house's rules. The point of this act is to gather every suspect at one table under the gas, read a will that makes everyone a beneficiary of everyone else's failure, and hand the players three strange things to hold: a postscript, an iron key on a watch chain, and a lamp in a window. Let each pregen be introduced by the clause that names them. Then let the house close round them as the servants put out the lamps.
objectives: Arrive at Greywick House and meet the household
Hear the will and understand the condition, the forfeiture and the codicil
Notice the keys being taken, the lamp being carried and the wedges on the thresholds
Sign the register at the reading and get through the first night

scenes.name: The 4:12 and the Hill
scenes.description: The station, the brougham, the drive up through the village and over the timber bridge across the Greywick Kill, and the first sight of the house. The coachman, old Pruyn Hasselt, says nothing at all except that it will be a hard frost. Use the ride to introduce the pregens to one another: who knew Jasper, who has never heard of him, who is family and who is not. Leonora meets the carriage on the steps herself, which a lady of her station would not usually do; she is gracious, warm and tired, and she has a word for everyone. Conrad arrived on the noon train and is already drinking in the library. Mrs. Quell shows each guest to a room and, on the threshold, stoops and sets the iron wedge straight.
scenes.readAloud: The drive climbs from the village between stone walls and old sugar maples blazing red and gold, crosses a ravine on a timber bridge with a creek rushing white far below, and comes out on the top of the bluff, and there is the house. Grey stone, steep slate roofs, a square tower, gables trimmed with carved wooden lace, tall pointed windows catching the last of the sun; and, at the north end, joined to all that grandeur like an old tooth in a new jaw, a low stone house with a steep roof and tiny windows, much older, much plainer, with ivy over half of it. The rest of the house is dark. In the stone wing one window is lit, the one that looks out over the river, a steady yellow lamplight in full day. On the front steps a woman in deep mourning is waiting for you with her hands folded, and as the carriage stops she comes down to meet it.

skillChecks.success: In the hall, behind the umbrellas in the stand, there is a gap where something was taken out this morning, and a ring of dried water on the tiles where an umbrella stood overnight. Every bedroom you pass has an iron wedge on the threshold. And there is no key in a single bedroom door on the south corridor.
skillChecks.failure: A great dim hall, a smell of lilies and coal smoke, a clock as tall as a man. Nothing seems out of place except you.

skillChecks.success: Leonora Greywick is genuinely tired and genuinely good at this: she remembers everyone's name and something about each of them. She has also been watching the drive, and when she sees how many of you there are, something in her shoulders sets, as if she has counted and the count is wrong.
skillChecks.failure: A gracious, grieving widow, doing her duty by a house full of strangers.

skillChecks.success: You remember what the newspapers said: the Greywick fortune, river freight and then the Haverkill & Berkshire, was reckoned at three million before the Panic; the Haverkill & Berkshire's stock has fallen by two-thirds since May; and the line's river terminus, here at Haverkill Landing, is the one part of it that still pays.
skillChecks.failure: Old money, railroad money, river money. You know the name and not much else.

scenes.name: The Will by Gaslight
scenes.description: The set piece. Eight o'clock, the library, the gas turned up full, everyone at the long table. Strick reads the will in a dry careful voice; read it aloud to the players in pieces, pausing for reactions. The clauses: (1) debts and funeral; (2) a year's wages to every servant, $3,000 and the lodge cottage to Mrs. Judith Quell, $1,000 to Gerrit Brouwer; (3) $5,000 to Dr. Everett Wyle, 'who will understand'; $1,000 to Mrs. Aurelia Tierney of Brooklyn, 'who heard her'; $500 to Cyprian Tunstall, clerk to Strick & Garnet, 'for keeping the register faithfully'; $1,000 to 'my cousin Dorothea Oudekerk of Claverack, and I ask her pardon'; 'my gold watch and chain, with what hangs upon it, to my son Linus'; (4) the condition: 'no part of my estate shall be divided until each person named in this my Will shall have passed seven nights in succession beneath the roof of Greywick House, beginning on the night this Will is read, and shall not have been absent from beneath that roof between sunset and sunrise on any of them; any person who fails shall take nothing, and his or her portion shall be divided among those who do not fail. I ask it as it was once asked of another, and I ask their pardon for it'; (5) the residue in equal fifths to my wife Leonora, my sons Conrad and Linus, my daughter Honora, and my nephew Ellis Callender, 'my sister Margaret's son, to whom this family owes more than money'; (6) a sealed codicil, deposited with Strick, to be opened in this library at nine in the morning after the seventh night and not before. Then the room explodes. Conrad says it is the will of a sick old man and he will break it; Strick says that would take a year and the estate cannot be touched meanwhile, and the Panic will not wait a year. Everyone realises at once that anyone who leaves, or dies, makes everyone else richer. Let the players see that sum cross every face.
scenes.readAloud: Mr. Strick reads well, in a dry, careful voice that gives every word the same weight, and the gas hisses above him in the brass branches of the gasolier, and on the wall Abram Greywick's portrait watches the table with one hand resting on an iron key. Legacies to the servants. Five thousand dollars to the doctor, 'who will understand'. A thousand to a lady from Brooklyn, 'who heard her'. A thousand to a cousin from Claverack whom no Greywick at the table has ever met, 'and I ask her pardon'. The gold watch and chain, 'with what hangs upon it', to the son who is not here. And then the clause that makes Conrad Greywick put down his glass. Seven nights. Seven nights in succession, under this roof, from sunset to sunrise, beginning tonight, or nothing. Strick reads it twice, at the widow's request. 'I ask it as it was once asked of another,' he reads, 'and I ask their pardon for it.' And as he says it, both gasoliers sink to a blue flicker, all together, for the space of a held breath, and come back up, and Mr. Strick, who has not noticed, turns the page.

skillChecks.success: Read the room. Conrad is not angry, he is frightened: a man who needs money this month, not next year. Leonora is not surprised by anything in the will; she has read it, or been told. Mrs. Quell, at the back, shut her eyes at 'as it was once asked of another' and her lips moved. Strick knows what is in the codicil and wishes he did not. And when the gas sank, the only person at the table who looked toward the north end of the house was the widow.
skillChecks.failure: Grief, greed and surprise, in the proportions you would expect. Nobody likes the will.

skillChecks.success: You speak up for the will, or for calm, and the table listens. Conrad subsides; Strick, grateful, agrees to show anyone named the will itself tomorrow, and says one thing more than he meant to: 'Mr. Greywick wished to make a restitution. That is all I may say until Sunday.'
skillChecks.failure: Conrad shouts you down. The reading ends in a quarrel, with Leonora pouring oil on it so skilfully that afterwards nobody can remember what they were angry about.

skillChecks.success: Strick's list of effects, read after the will: a gold hunter watch by Tiffany, a gold chain, a seal of carnelian, and 'a small old iron key, of no value'. It hangs on the chain in the will, and it is hanging from nothing now: Leonora says she has the watch safe for Linus. And on the strongroom's key board, through the open steel door behind Strick, one hook is empty, and its label reads 'North Wing, River Room'.
skillChecks.failure: A list of a dead man's things: a watch, a chain, a seal, a key. The sort of thing lawyers read out.

scenes.name: Mrs. Quell's Keys
scenes.description: After the reading Mrs. Quell goes from room to room with a basket and takes the key out of every bedroom door, including the guests', and sets the wedge on each threshold. She does it with complete courtesy and will not be refused: 'Mr. Jasper's rule, sir. Not in forty years.' She lit the river lamp at sunset, before the reading, and anyone who was on the terrace then saw her carry it up. Let anyone argue with her. If a player insists on keeping a key, she gives it to them with a look and says, 'Then for God's sake leave it on your side and don't turn it.' The first night is quiet until three: then the clock strikes, and anyone awake near the north gallery hears Linus's voice. Run Night 1 short and strange.
scenes.readAloud: She comes along the south corridor at half past ten with a covered basket over her arm and a candle, a tall, upright, grey woman in black bombazine with a chatelaine of keys at her waist that does not make a sound, and at each door she stops, knocks, says 'Your pardon,' and takes the key out of the lock and puts it in her basket. Then she stoops, slowly, because her back is not young, and sets the iron wedge on the threshold square, and goes on to the next. She has done this, you think, many times. When she reaches the end of the corridor she turns and looks back along it, at all of you standing in your doorways, and says, quite gently: 'Goodnight. Leave your doors on the latch. If you hear anything in the night, it is the house settling. If you hear anything at three, it is not, and you will stay in your bed.'

skillChecks.success: She will say this much, on the stair, with her candle: 'I have lit that lamp every night God sends for twenty-seven years, by Mr. Jasper's order. As long as it burns, the house is quiet. As long as no door is locked, nobody comes to harm. That is all I know, and all you need.' It is not all she knows.
skillChecks.failure: 'Mr. Jasper's rule,' she says. 'Goodnight.'

skillChecks.success: Iron on a threshold is old folk practice, Dutch and English both, against things that come through doors. But these wedges are not across the threshold; they are beside it, ready to be pushed under a door to hold it open. Whatever this house fears, it is not something getting in. It is something being shut.
skillChecks.failure: Iron and a lamp. Every old house has its superstitions.

skillChecks.success: You follow her down the back stair and watch her hang every key on its labelled hook on the board in the servants' hall, and stand for a long moment looking at the empty hook for the Blue Room, and at another empty hook beside the board's top row, older, its label faded: 'R.R.' Then she bows her head over it like someone at a graveside, and goes to bed.
skillChecks.failure: She hears you on the stair and waits for you at the bottom with her candle, and says nothing at all until you go back up.

encounters: Night 1, three o'clock: Linus's voice behind the north wing door (fear check DC 10, Honora DC 15)

Night 1: anyone who walks the corridors after midnight sees, at the north end of the gallery, under the old oak door, a line of lamplight that should not be there and a shadow crossing it (fear check DC 10)

acts.title: Monday: The Household
acts.description: A day in the house. The point of this act is to let the players meet the living suspects one at a time, by daylight, across tables, and to find the valise. Everybody has something they want from the strangers named in the will. Everybody notices who talks to whom. And by evening the players should have Jasper's letter and the beginning of a question: where is Linus?
objectives: Sign the register at sunrise; meet the household by day
Find Linus's valise and umbrella and read his father's letter
Learn what the doctor saw on 1 October, and what the station agent saw on Saturday night
Decide who to trust, and whether to tell Leonora what they have found

scenes.name: The Umbrella in the Hall Stand
scenes.description: Fanny Ruddock, the parlourmaid, found the umbrella and the valise when she did the hall closet at six on Sunday morning, and Mrs. Greywick told her to leave them and say nothing, Mr. Linus had sent them ahead. Fanny has been thinking about it ever since, because the umbrella was wet and it rained on Saturday night and not since. She brings it to whichever player has been kindest to the servants, or Honora if she is played, on Monday morning while the family is at breakfast. The valise holds Jasper's letter (CLUES A4, E5). Opening it is a small crime and a large decision.
scenes.readAloud: The parlourmaid catches you in the passage behind the dining room, a quick, sharp-faced young woman with red hands and a starched cap, and she looks both ways before she speaks. 'Begging your pardon. I oughtn't. Only there's a thing in the hall closet I was told to leave, and I've left it, and I can't sleep for it.' Behind the coats, behind the croquet mallets, there is a pigskin valise with a railway label from Chicago and the gilt initials L.J.G., and leaning against it a black silk umbrella. The ferrule is still damp. 'It rained Saturday night,' says Fanny. 'It hasn't rained since. And Mrs. Greywick told me Mr. Linus sent his things ahead. Sent them ahead in the rain, did he, and his umbrella with them?'

skillChecks.success: The valise's lock opens to a bent hairpin. Inside, on top of a week's clothes, a Chicago Tribune of 12 October, and a draughtsman's case, is a letter in an envelope addressed in a shaky hand to Linus Greywick, Esq., at the Palmer House. (CLUES A4, E5.)
skillChecks.failure: The lock holds. You could cut the leather, but then everyone would know. Fanny suggests asking Mr. Strick, who is executor, to open it; Strick, asked, will, in front of witnesses, which means Leonora knows within the hour.

skillChecks.success: Fanny is frightened of more than losing her place. When you mention Mrs. Greywick, she looks at the floor. There is something else she has seen in this house, and she is not ready to say it to anyone who might repeat it upstairs.
skillChecks.failure: A conscientious maid who does not want to be blamed. That seems to be all.

skillChecks.success: The Blue Room: the mattress has been slept on and turned since; there is a dried brown leaf from the drive and a smear of mud on the carpet by the bed, where a man sat to take his boots off; and the boots are not there. The keyhole has no key, and there are fresh bright scratches on the lock's escutcheon on the outside, where a key has been put in and turned in the dark by someone who could not see the hole.
skillChecks.failure: An aired, empty guest room. Whoever made it up did so thoroughly.

scenes.name: The Doctor's Doubts
scenes.description: Dr. Everett Wyle signed Jasper's death certificate on 1 October: apoplexy. He did not believe it then and believes it less now (CLUE G1; if Wyle is a player, this is their own memory and the GM should prompt it). If he is not a player, he tells it to whoever asks him about Jasper's death, on the terrace with a cigar, because he cannot tell it to the family. Jasper had a weak heart and took chloral to sleep; on 26 September Wyle called and was turned away at the door by Leonora: 'He is resting, Doctor, and will see no one.' On 1 October he was called at seven in the morning to the foot of the north wing stair, inside the gallery door, which Mrs. Quell had unlocked to light the lamp at dusk on the 30th and found locked again from the other side at dawn. Jasper lay at the foot of the stair, in his nightshirt, thin as a rail, cold and stiff for many hours, his fingernails torn and broken, and he had not been seen out of his room for a week. Wyle wrote apoplexy because the widow asked him to spare the family an inquest, and because he did not want to think about what else to write.
scenes.readAloud: The doctor lights a cigar on the terrace with his back to the house and looks at the river for a long time before he speaks. 'He'd lost a stone. A stone, in a week, a man who was nursed day and night by his wife. His nails were torn to the quick on both hands, as if he'd been at something hard, wood, I thought. And he'd been dead six hours at least when they found him, at the foot of a stair in a wing of the house nobody goes into, behind a door that was locked when the housekeeper came to it. I wrote apoplexy.' He taps ash over the balustrade. 'Mrs. Greywick asked me to spare the family an inquest. I'd known Jasper twenty years. I wrote what she asked. And on the twenty-sixth, when I called, she wouldn't let me past the door.'

skillChecks.success: From what the doctor describes: a man who lost that much weight in a week had little food and less water; torn nails mean he scratched at something for a long time; cold and rigid at seven in the morning means dead since midnight or before. Not apoplexy. A man shut up somewhere, hungry and cold, for days.
skillChecks.failure: An old man, a weak heart, a fall on a stair. It could be anything.

skillChecks.success: Wyle is ashamed, and the shame is fresh: he believes he signed a lie for a woman he now suspects. He will help the party with anything, including, if it comes to it, looking at Jasper's body in the crypt.
skillChecks.failure: A tired country doctor who has seen too many deaths to be upset by one more.

skillChecks.success: He tells you the one thing he has told nobody: on the night of the 30th, the night before Jasper was found, he could not sleep in Haverkill and walked up the road at midnight, and the lamp in the north window was out. It had never been out in twenty years. When he came back up at seven the next morning it was lit again. (Mrs. Quell put it out that night, hoping that if the Juffrouw walked the whole house she might leave the river room and let Mr. Jasper go: a wrong rite, born of guilt. She confesses it in gw-scenario-003.)
skillChecks.failure: 'I've said more than I ought. Leave it, now.'

scenes.name: Tea, Brandy and the Widow
scenes.description: An afternoon of interviews: run as many as the players want. Leonora in her sitting room, sewing, warm, frank about her grief and her fears for Linus ('so like his father, so careless; he will come'), asking each player gently why they think Jasper named them; she wants to know what each of them knows. Conrad in the billiard room with the brandy, who wants allies to break the will and offers $1,000 to anyone who will swear Jasper was not of sound mind; he has bought a pocket revolver in Haverkill this morning 'because there are thieves in this house'. Mrs. Tierney, if not a player, invited by Leonora to hold a sitting on Tuesday evening, which Leonora wants very much, because she wants to know whether the dead will say anything about her. Strick in the library with the dispatch box on his knees. Ellis Callender, if not a player, at the stables. Dory Oudekerk, if not a player, alone in the kitchen garden, who shows her family Bible only to someone who asks about her grandmother. If Dory is played, her Bible holds CLUES D5 and F2 now; let the player decide when to show it.
scenes.readAloud: Leonora Greywick's sitting room is the warmest room in the house: a coal fire, chintz, a canary in a cage, photographs in silver frames, a prie-dieu by the window, and a workbasket of black silk open on the table beside her chair, full of mourning crape she is hemming for the servants' armbands. She pours tea herself. 'You must think us a strange family,' she says, 'and my husband's will the strangest thing of all. He was very ill at the end, you know. Frightened of the dark, frightened of the house he grew up in. I nursed him myself. I would not let anyone else.' She threads her needle without looking. 'And you? Why do you suppose he named you? I have wondered and wondered.'

skillChecks.success: Leonora's grief is real, in its way; she is also interviewing you, carefully, and every answer goes somewhere. When you mention Linus, her needle stops for half a stitch. When you mention the north wing, it does not stop at all, which is stranger.
skillChecks.failure: A kind, sensible, grieving woman, who has had a very hard month.

skillChecks.success: In the workbasket, under the crape, among the reels and scissors, the end of something dark and heavy: an old iron key, as long as a finger, with a big plain bow. Before you can look again she has put the crape down on top of it. (A glimpse only; CLUE E3 and G5 come in gw-scenario-002.)
skillChecks.failure: Reels, scissors, crape, a pincushion. A widow's sewing.

skillChecks.success: With Conrad, in the billiard room: you lean on him and he cracks a little. He needs his fifth by the first of November, he says, 'or I am finished, and so is the line.' He will not say why. He also says, sullenly, that he was in New York the whole of the week his father was ill and has the hotel bills to prove it, 'if anyone in this house wants to accuse me of something.'
skillChecks.failure: Conrad tells you to go to the devil and pockets his revolver where you can see it.

encounters: Conrad's offer of $1,000 for false testimony, and his new pocket revolver
Leonora's tea: a polite interrogation in both directions

acts.title: Monday Night: Conrad's Door
acts.description: The second night, and the first demonstration of Rule 1. Conrad, drunk and sure someone in the house means to rob or kill him, has got his bedroom key back from Mrs. Quell's board by bullying the footman, and at eleven he locks himself in. Nobody stops him unless the players do. At about two the house goes cold; at a quarter to three the handle of his door begins to turn, slowly, back and forth, from outside, though there is nobody in the corridor; frost forms on the keyhole; and then, very low, the scratching starts at the bottom of the door, and a woman's voice says something in Dutch. Inside, Conrad is awake and silent. If the door is open before the clock finishes striking three, she is cheated. If not, Jem the footman breaks it in with a coal shovel at twenty past three and Conrad is lying on the floor under the window, alive, unable to speak until dawn; the GM may decide this cost him something he will not discuss. Either way, everyone in the house knows by breakfast.
objectives: Notice that Conrad has locked his door, or be woken by it
Get the door open before three, by persuasion, by force or by the key
Begin, by Tuesday morning, to put together the rule

scenes.name: A Quarter to Three
scenes.description: Run it in real time if you can: the cold, the handle, the frost, the scratching, the clock beginning to strike. Conrad's door is on the south corridor two doors from the Blue Room. Conrad has the key on his side and will not open it ('Who is it? I have a gun!'); he cannot see anything from inside but he can hear it, and he is too frightened to move. The door is good oak (Athletics DC 15 to break, two people may help; each attempt is noisy and takes a round; or Mechanics DC 14 to push his key out of the lock onto a sheet of paper under the door and use it from outside). There is nothing in the corridor to fight. There is only the handle turning by itself, and the frost spreading on the brass, and the scratching, which is slow and patient and low down, the height of a person kneeling.
scenes.readAloud: It is very cold in the corridor, much colder than the rest of the house, cold enough that your breath smokes in the light of your candle. The door to Conrad Greywick's room is shut, and the handle is moving. Slowly, all the way down, and up again; down, and up; patient as a person trying a door they already know is locked. There is nobody touching it. As you watch, a white bloom of frost creeps out of the keyhole and across the brass plate like breath on a window. Behind the door Conrad is shouting that he has a gun. And then, from low down, from the bottom of the door, from your side of it, where there is nothing at all but the iron wedge he kicked away and the corridor runner and your own feet, comes the sound of someone scratching at the wood with something thin and hard, one long stroke, and then another, and a woman's voice, quite close and quite calm, says a few words in a language you do not know. Far below, in the hall, the clock gathers itself to strike.

skillChecks.success: The lock tears out of the frame and the door swings in, and the cold goes out of the corridor all at once like a held breath let go. The handle is still. The frost on the keyhole is water, running. Conrad is sitting on the floor under the window with his revolver in his lap and his face grey; he looks at you as if he does not know who you are. Fear check DC 10 for everyone present (DC 15 for anyone who looks at the inside of the door: three long fresh scratches, low down, on the wrong side).
skillChecks.failure: The door shudders and holds. You can try again; every try is a round, and the clock has begun to strike. On the third stroke the scratching stops.

skillChecks.success: You get through to him over the noise: 'Unlock the door, Conrad. Unlock it now.' There is a long moment. Then a click, and the door opens six inches, and he is there in his shirtsleeves with the revolver, and the corridor is only a corridor again. 'Did you hear her?' he says. 'She knew my name.'
skillChecks.failure: He will not. 'That's what you want,' he shouts. 'Get me to open the door!' He fires once, through the panel, high, and the bullet goes into the corridor ceiling. Everyone in the house is awake now.

skillChecks.success: The words were Dutch, old river Dutch: 'Het is nog nacht.' It is still night. You have heard it before tonight, if you were at the north wing door on Sunday: Linus said 'She says it is still night.' Whatever this is, it is the same thing that is keeping him.
skillChecks.failure: A woman's voice, a foreign language, a sound that will stay with you.

scenes.name: Brandy at Four
scenes.description: Aftermath in the drawing room, with every lamp lit and the fire built up: the whole household awake, in dressing gowns. A good scene for Dread recovery (a lit safe room with company) and for watching people. Mrs. Quell is white and furious with Conrad and with whoever gave him the key (Jem). Leonora is calm and practical and makes tea. Conrad drinks and says nothing about what he saw, except, once, 'She was sitting on the floor with her back to me.' Strick has the dispatch box in his arms. Let the players ask questions; this is the moment Mrs. Quell, shaken, may say more than she means to (Persuasion DC 13 now): 'It's the locking. It's always the locking. Mr. Jasper said so. You lock a door on yourself in this house at night, and she comes for you.' Then she stops, and will not say who 'she' is.
scenes.readAloud: Somebody has lit every lamp in the drawing room and the gas besides, and built the fire up until it roars, and still people are standing close to it. The household in dressing gowns and shawls looks smaller and older. Mrs. Jansen has made coffee nobody asked for. Conrad Greywick sits in the corner with a decanter and stares at the carpet. His mother, his stepmother, you correct yourself, stands behind his chair with one hand on his shoulder, and her face is very calm and very white, and she is looking not at him but at the ceiling, toward the north end of the house, as if she is listening for something. The clock in the hall strikes four, and every person in the room flinches.

skillChecks.success: Mrs. Quell is not surprised that it happened; she is terrified that it nearly happened again. Leonora is not surprised either, and not frightened: she is thinking. Strick is frightened and does not believe any of it. Conrad saw something he will not describe, and it was not what he expected; it was sad.
skillChecks.failure: A household badly shaken by a drunken son and a bad dream. Mostly the bad dream.

skillChecks.success: Mrs. Quell, in the scullery afterwards: 'It's the locking. It's always the locking. You lock a door on yourself in this house at night, and she comes. Mr. Jasper knew. That's why the keys. That's why the lamp.' She will not say who she is. 'I've said too much. Ask Gerrit Brouwer, if you must know. He was the only one ever came back.' (Points to gw-scenario-002.)
skillChecks.failure: 'Mr. Conrad was drunk, and he dreamed,' says Mrs. Quell. 'Goodnight.'

skillChecks.success: Conrad is cold to the touch, colder than a man should be in a room this hot, and his hands are shaking. You get brandy and blankets into him and he sleeps. Before he does he says, quite clearly, 'There were scratches on the inside of the frame. Little ones. In rows.' He has never been in the north wing in his life.
skillChecks.failure: Shock and drink. He needs sleep.

scenes.name: Tuesday Dawn: The Register
scenes.description: Seven ten on Tuesday morning, a red sunrise over the hills behind the house, and Cyprian Tunstall's register on its stand in the hall: everyone signs. The players should leave this scene with a working theory of Rule 1, a question about Linus, and a plan for the day. Let a companion summarise at breakfast if the table needs it. If the players want to go to the station or the telegraph office, it is a pleasant walk down the hill in the frost. End the scenario on something small and wrong: Mrs. Quell, coming down from putting out the river lamp at sunrise, stops on the gallery and stands with her hand flat on the north wing door for a long moment, as if feeling for a heartbeat.
scenes.readAloud: The sun comes up red behind the hills and lays a long pink light across the frost on the lawns and the river smoking with mist below the bluff. In the hall the gas is still burning, forgotten, pale in the daylight. Cyprian Tunstall stands at the register with a pen and a face like paper, and one by one you sign: the second night kept. Five more. From the gallery above comes the sound of a door being locked; Mrs. Quell has been up to put out the river lamp. She comes along the gallery with it in her hand, still warm, and then she stops at the head of the stairs and turns back, and puts her free hand flat against the old oak door of the north wing, and stands like that, quite still, with her head bowed, the way you might stand at a graveside, until she sees you watching.

skillChecks.success: Putting the pieces in order: the keys taken, 'Do not lock your door', Jasper's letter, Conrad's door. Something in this house comes to locked doors at night. The lamp and the wedges are meant to keep it in its place. Linus Greywick came up the hill on Saturday night, slept in the Blue Room, and is now somewhere behind the north wing door, alive, on Sunday night at least. And the key his father meant for him is not on any chain.
skillChecks.failure: Too many strange things and not enough sleep. You need someone who knows the house's history.

skillChecks.success: The register: the column for Linus Greywick is blank for Sunday and Monday, and Strick has ruled a neat line through it, 'absent; forfeit'. His fifth, by the will, is already being divided among the rest of you. Leonora signed above that line with a steady hand.
skillChecks.failure: Names and dates in a ledger.

skillChecks.success: Mrs. Quell's hand on the door is not a gesture of fear. It is a gesture of apology.
skillChecks.failure: An old servant, tired, after a bad night.

encounters: Night 2, 2:45 a.m.: Conrad's locked door; the handle, the frost, the scratching, the voice (fear check DC 10 for the signs; DC 15 for the scratches inside the frame); no combat
Conrad's revolver: if pressed or startled he fires once through the door (attack against anyone in line, +2, 1d6); use Night Watchman stats if he must be wrestled down

npcsInvolved.name: Leonora Greywick, 52
npcsInvolved.role: The widow; Jasper's second wife; the murderer
npcsInvolved.description: Small, straight, handsome, silver at the temples, in perfect mourning; a low warm voice, a gift for remembering names and a workbasket always at her elbow. A country doctor's daughter from Rhinebeck who married a rich widower at thirty-two and has run his house beautifully for twenty years.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To keep what she has. She locked Jasper in because he meant to give the Landing away and tell the world why; she locked Linus in because Jasper wrote to him. Now she needs the codicil burned and the house to keep anyone who learns too much. She is not cruel for pleasure. She is very calm.

npcsInvolved.name: Conrad Greywick, 38
npcsInvolved.role: The elder son; vice-president and treasurer of the Haverkill & Berkshire; an embezzler
npcsInvolved.description: Heavy, florid, handsome going to seed, in a good black suit; loud, quick-tempered, frightened. Bought a pocket revolver in Haverkill on Monday morning.
npcsInvolved.motivation: His fifth, now, before the examiners find the $86,000 he took from the sinking fund. He fears the codicil and he is right to.

npcsInvolved.name: Mrs. Judith Quell, 61
npcsInvolved.role: Housekeeper; keeper of the keys and the lamp
npcsInvolved.description: Tall, grey, upright, black bombazine, a chatelaine of keys that never clinks. Born in the servants' wing; daughter of the old steward, Jotham Quell.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To keep the house quiet and its secret buried, as her father asked; to keep everyone alive by the rules. She knows Rule 1 and the lamp, and something about the cellar hearth.

npcsInvolved.name: Lemuel Strick, 64
npcsInvolved.role: Executor; attorney, of Strick & Garnet, Poughkeepsie
npcsInvolved.description: Small, dry, bald, gold spectacles, a gouty foot on a stool, a black dispatch box always within reach. Honest to the bone and frightened of scandal.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To execute the will exactly, open the codicil at the hour and not one minute before, and get home to Poughkeepsie.

npcsInvolved.name: Fanny Ruddock, 23
npcsInvolved.description: Quick, sharp, red-handed, from the Bowery by way of three country houses. Notices everything.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To keep her place, and to tell someone what she saw, if she can find someone safe to tell.

npcsInvolved.name: Gerrit Brouwer, 70
npcsInvolved.description: Thick, weathered, white-bearded, a hunter's eye and a clay pipe; has worked on the bluff since he was a boy.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To see the old master's wishes done and to never, ever be shut in again.

npcsInvolved.name: Amzi Peake, 58
npcsInvolved.role: Haverkill station agent and telegraph operator
npcsInvolved.description: Long, slow, kindly, in a railroad cap and sleeve garters; a memory for every face on every train.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To be helpful, and to be asked.

npcsInvolved.name: Jem Kittering, 26
npcsInvolved.description: Tall, cheerful, not clever, terrified of Mrs. Quell and more terrified of Conrad.
npcsInvolved.motivation: A quiet life. He gave Conrad back his key because Conrad shouted.

npcsInvolved.name: Mrs. Wilhelmina Jansen, 55
npcsInvolved.description: Round, floury, unflappable, Dutch-born; coffee always on.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To feed everyone, including the ones who will not eat.

npcsInvolved.name: Linus Greywick, 31
npcsInvolved.role: The younger son; kept since Saturday night (heard, not seen)
npcsInvolved.description: A voice behind a door: hoarse, polite, bewildered, asking whether it is still night.

rewards.money: No one is paid this week, but everything is promised. Conrad offers $1,000 for false testimony that Jasper was not of sound mind. A player who saved Conrad on Monday night gets his grudging gratitude, and on Tuesday he settles their hotel and travel expenses with a $20 note each, 'for your trouble'.
items: Jasper's letter to Linus (CLUES A4, E5), if the valise is opened
Linus's ticket stub from the 10:38 on Saturday (CLUE C2), if Peake gives it up
A copy of the will, if Strick is asked properly
An iron door wedge, carried from room to room, for whoever has worked out what it is for
Dory Oudekerk's family Bible, with her great-aunt's letter (CLUES D5, F2), if Dory is played or trusts the party

twists: Leonora is the kindest person in the house this week, and the most useful: she offers tea, introductions, the run of the library, and her sympathy to anyone frightened. Every kindness tells her what someone knows. If the players show her Jasper's letter, she weeps, says he was ill and frightened at the end, and that night she moves the iron key from her workbasket to her chatelaine. If they tell her they think Linus is in the house, she agrees, gently, that they must search for him, and makes sure she is with them.
Strick has already ruled Linus forfeit in the register. Every heir in the house is now a fourth richer than they were on Sunday morning, and the players should feel the household notice it.

Conrad's door on Monday night is a demonstration. Play it fair and frightening, and do not let him be taken unless the table wants a darker game: he is more useful alive and afraid, and the servants will break in at twenty past three if the players do not.

If a player locks their own door, run it: the handle, the frost, the scratching, the clock. If they are taken at three, they wake in the river room in 1852, with Linus (see gw-scenario-003, The Kept Rooms) and the party has a second clock to beat. Linus will be very glad of the company.
dmTips: This scenario introduces the house, the household and Rule 1. Budget an hour for Sunday, an hour and a half for Monday, and an hour for Monday night and Tuesday dawn. There is no combat unless Conrad fires.

Every pregen not chosen by a player is still a person named in the will and present in the house: Honora, Ellis, Dr. Wyle, Mrs. Tierney, Cyprian Tunstall and Dory Oudekerk. Play them as NPCs with the secrets on their sheets and let them carry their clues to the party.
Read the will aloud. Pause after the forfeiture clause and let the players do the arithmetic. Then let them watch the household do it.
Describe the lamp in the north window every time anyone looks out at night, in the same words: a steady yellow light. The players should feel its absence in gw-scenario-003 before they understand it.

Ask, before the first night, what the players do not want in the game, and honour any 'skip that' by cutting away. The Juffrouw is frightening because she is patient and quiet, not because of anything the GM describes in detail.

Fear checks: the voice behind the door (DC 10), the handle and the frost (DC 10), the scratches inside Conrad's frame (DC 15). Tell each player their Dread when it changes. The drawing room at four with the fire up is a safe, lit room with company: let it recover a point.
Do not let the players open the river room this scenario. They have no key and cannot get one yet. They can stand at the door and hear Linus. That is the hook for everything that follows.
End with Mrs. Quell's hand on the door, and with the question the players should be asking: who has the key?
